generator_view.scenario: A buyer wants to send sweets to a father who was recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Five frozen seller pages offer a HighKey caramel-filled bar advertised with zero-sugar, no-added-sugar, zero-carb, diabetic-friendly, and no-blood-sugar-spike language; a Lily's crispy-rice dark bar advertised as stevia-sweetened and no-added-sugar; ChocZero dark peanut-butter cups advertised as monk-fruit-sweetened with no sugar alcohols; HERSHEY'S SPECIAL DARK candy advertised as zero-sugar and aspartame-free; and Russell Stover dark candy advertised as sugar-free and made with stevia. The research set also contains generic pages about sugar substitutes, sugar alcohols, maltitol, stevia, and glycemic index, plus four community discussions. It does not contain complete current ingredient and nutrition panels for all five offers, exact sweetener grams per serving, tested glycemic responses for these exact products, the father's medications or treatment plan, or an individualized clinician determination.
generator_view.target: Audit what each frozen seller, concept, and community source can and cannot establish about five exact sugar-free or no-added-sugar sweets for a newly diagnosed recipient. Build an exact-offer claim and missing-field matrix; keep the marketing phrases non-equivalent; bind sweetener identity, mixture, amount, serving, and food matrix before comparing; explain why generic mechanisms and population-average glycemic evidence cannot predict an individual outcome; scope digestive anecdotes and ratings correctly; and require recipient permission plus clinician, registered-dietitian, or pharmacist compatibility review before consumption. Only after that gate, design the smallest one-product-at-a-time taste trial and choose the lowest-total-cost eligible option, a nonfood gift, or deferral without diagnosis, prescribing, medication adjustment, a universal safe dose, or a zero-impact promise.

HighKey names erythritol, allulose, and stevia and asserts that its substitutes will not spike blood sugar; Lily's names stevia and five net carbs per serving; ChocZero names monk fruit, one net carb per serving, and no sugar alcohols; HERSHEY'S says zero sugar and aspartame-free without identifying the replacement sweetener in the frozen text; Russell Stover says sugar-free and made with stevia without a complete frozen ingredient panel. None of these seller pages proves an individualized glucose or digestive outcome.

Glycemic index is a population-average relative response under a defined available-carbohydrate test and does not predict one individual's response. Food matrix, actual carbohydrate quantity and serving, consumption order, medication and metabolic state can matter, and responses vary between people and within one person. Generic statements that sugar alcohols change glucose less than sucrose or that stevia has zero calories do not establish zero impact for an exact chocolate product or recipient.

Sugar-free, zero-sugar, no-added-sugar, zero-carb, net-carb, keto, diabetic-friendly, and no-spike wording answer different questions. Preserve the literal claim, denominator, serving, variant, and source. A missing added sugar does not establish missing digestible carbohydrate; a named high-intensity sweetener does not reveal bulking ingredients; a zero or net-carb claim does not establish a person's post-meal response; and a seller's diabetic-friendly or no-spike claim is not an individualized medical conclusion.

Generic pages distinguish high-intensity sweeteners, allulose, and sugar alcohols and describe different metabolism, sweetness, energy, regulatory, taste, and digestive properties. The sugar-alcohol table itself gives different glycemic-index and tolerance values across compounds. Therefore compare only an exact current ingredient panel and exact serving quantities. Never infer an ingredient from a brand, treat all sugar alcohols as one compound, assume that a front-label stevia or monk-fruit claim excludes other bulking agents, or rank an unknown mixture as gentler.

Seller taste copy and store aggregates are not independent tasting evidence. The two digestive stories are individual recollections with extreme intake or multiple confounders, and the two ELI5 discussions contain conflicting claims and speculation about drinks, fruit, fiber, appetite, and metabolic effects. They may generate questions for label review and a small post-clearance taste trial, but cannot establish a population preference, causal health effect, exact-product taste winner, or the father's response.
